definition: A situation where work processes are spread across multiple disconnected tools, leading to inefficiency and lack of visibility.
extendedDefinition: Workflow fragmentation describes work spread across disconnected tools, where no single system holds the full picture of a process. Its costs are silent but compounding: information lives in unlinked places, status is unclear, handoffs break, and reporting requires manual assembly. Fragmentation typically emerges when teams add point solutions without considering integration, and it intensifies as the organization grows. Buyers should assess their own stack for fragmentation before purchasing, because a new tool can either consolidate workflows or add another disconnected island. Evaluation should focus on how candidate products connect to existing systems, share context, and support end-to-end visibility. Consolidation projects reduce fragmentation by replacing several tools with platforms that cover broader workflows, but they carry migration risk that should be planned. The goal of healthy software portfolios is processes that flow across tools with clear ownership and minimal manual handoff.
